title: I Made My First Educational App, and It’s Just One Question
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Phillip Alcock offers a beginner walkthrough for teachers who want to start making their own educational apps, estimated at fifteen to twenty minutes. The project is a single HTML file that displays a solar system quiz question with three answer buttons that do not yet check answers, so the focus stays on creating a file, opening it in a browser and editing the content. He explains headings, paragraphs, buttons and the html, head and body structure in plain terms, then breaks the work into four steps, each with what you should have, a check before continuing, and what to do if it fails. The final step has the reader swap in a question of their own and refresh the browser. A completion checklist closes the post and points toward adding JavaScript feedback in a later project.
points: A working educational page can be built with nothing but a plain-text editor and a browser, and the only skills required are saving a file with the correct .html extension and keeping tags paired.
Each step lists what you should have, what to check, and what to do if it fails, which makes the lesson usable by a complete beginner.
Deliberately leaving the buttons inert keeps the first project small and sets up a later lesson on adding JavaScript to check answers and show feedback.
Editing the question and refreshing the browser teaches the core loop of changing content, saving and reloading.
quotes: The page will show a question about the solar system. Its buttons will appear on the screen, but they will not check answers yet.
For this first project, the focus is on creating a file, opening it and changing the content yourself.
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. A browser reads HTML and uses it to work out what each part of a page is.

The browser can tell that “Space Quiz” is a heading and “Choose one answer” is a paragraph because they use different HTML elements. You can change the words between the tags without changing the element itself.
A browser will let you select the button, but the HTML in this project does not tell it what to do next. In a later project, you could add JavaScript to check the answer and display feedback.
On Windows, if Notepad offers a Save as type option, choose All Files so the name does not end in .txt.
Keep the tags around the new text. Save the file, return to your browser and refresh the page.
